transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for fitting me in. I, um, well, I suppose I’m here because... goodness, where do I even start? My daughter was actually the one who said I should talk to someone, because I just feel like I’m always, always up and moving. You’d think at seventy years old, being retired and all, I’d have all the time in the world to just relax and put my feet up. But even on a supposedly quiet day, I am just constantly on the go. 

Like, just the other morning, I sat down with my tea to finally update the contact list for my garden club. I took over as secretary this spring, which is a lovely group of ladies, but keeping track of them is a full-time job on its own. Anyway, before I even got halfway through the names, I was up and digging through my knitting bag in the other room because I suddenly remembered a pattern I wanted to check. But then, before I could even find my measuring tape in the bag, I caught sight of the travel papers for our trip next month sitting on the dining table, and suddenly I’m pulling those out to check the hotel itinerary! 

It’s just... I’m bouncing from the garden club list to my knitting bag to the travel papers, and before I know it, the afternoon is completely gone and I haven’t really finished any one thing. It’s just this constant buzzing around the house. I'll walk into a room and start three different projects, and my husband just watches me go back and forth. I just don't really know why I can't just sit still and finish a simple chore like a normal person, you know? It's exhausting, quite frankly.
Do you feel like you're moving from one thing to another because you can't seem to settle or because you're trying to get a lot done?

Oh, that is a very good question. You know, I suppose people might look at me and think I’m just trying to be a busy bee and get a million chores done, but... well, honestly, it’s really because I just can't seem to settle. 

It's the strangest thing. If I have to sit still for too long—like if my husband puts on one of his long history documentaries in the evening, he just loves those World War II ones on PBS, and I do try to sit and watch them with him because it’s nice to spend that time together—but after maybe twenty or thirty minutes, I get this... this stirred-up feeling inside. It's almost like a little motor humming, and I just feel like I absolutely need to stand up and straighten something or go check on something. 

I'll tell him I'm just going to the kitchen for a glass of water, but really I just need to get up and go fluff the throw pillows in the den, or check if I remembered to lock the back door, or see if the African violets on the windowsill need watering. And once I'm up, of course, that's when I start bouncing around again. So it's not really that I have some grand master plan to be incredibly productive, though Lord knows there is always something to clean or organize in that house. It's more that my body just decides it's had enough of the chair and I have to move. Even at church, if the pastor's sermon goes on a bit too long, I get that exact same stirred-up feeling in my chest and I catch myself shifting around, just waiting until we can finally stand up for the last hymn. I just can't seem to turn that feeling off, no matter how much I tell myself to just relax.
Do you feel anxious or worried when you're sitting still and get that stirred-up feeling inside?

Oh, anxious? Worried? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like a... like a dread or a fear that something terrible is going to happen, you know? It's not like when I couldn't find my granddaughter at the county fair that one time—now that was anxiety! My heart was pounding out of my chest, I was sweating, I couldn't breathe right until I saw her over by the cotton candy stand with her uncle. No, this feeling when I'm sitting still, it's completely different from that. 

It's really just... physical, I suppose? Like an itch you can't scratch, or like when you've had way too much coffee, though I only ever have my one cup of decaf in the mornings now because regular coffee gives me terrible heartburn. But it's just this restless energy. I don't sit there thinking, "Oh dear, did I leave the stove on?" or "What if the roof leaks?" I just sit there and my legs want to move, and my arms want to do something, and my brain just says, "Up, up, up, time to go!" 

So it's not a worry. It's not my mind spinning with bad thoughts. It's just my body absolutely refusing to be still. My husband, bless him, he'll ask me sometimes, "What's wrong, dear? What are you fretting about?" when he sees me fidgeting during his programs. And I always have to tell him, "I'm not fretting about a single thing, George! I just can't sit in this recliner for one more second!" So, no, definitely not anxious, just... terribly, terribly restless.
Do you ever feel irritable when you're unable to move around or engage in activities?

Irritable? Oh, goodness, no, I wouldn't say irritable. I mean, I don't get snappy or mean with anyone just because I have to sit still. George, my husband, he’s the one who gets irritable if his back is acting up and he can’t get out to his woodworking shop in the garage, but me? No, I don't get cross. 

It’s just... well, like I was saying, it’s just that restless, humming feeling. I might sigh a bit, or shift my weight, or start tapping my foot—which I know can probably be a bit annoying to anyone sitting next to me, especially in a quiet church pew or when George is trying to listen to the narrator on his shows. But it's not because I'm mad or frustrated. I don't sit there feeling angry that I can't get up. I just sit there feeling like I *have* to get up. 

There was this one time, oh, it must have been last Thanksgiving, when my daughter insisted I sit at the head of the table and just let everyone else serve the meal and clear the plates. She meant well, she really did, she kept saying, "Mom, you cooked the turkey, you just sit and enjoy." And I tried, I really did try to just sit there while they bustled around clearing the good china—which, by the way, I only bring out for Thanksgiving and Easter because it has to be hand-washed, and nobody wants to do that every day. But anyway, as I sat there watching them, I wasn't irritable with them for making me sit. I just felt that motor running inside me, telling me to get up and help scrape the plates or put the leftover stuffing in the Tupperware. 

So, no, I wouldn't use the word irritable at all. I don't lose my temper or feel grumpy about it. It's really just that my body is so very eager to be doing *something*, anything at all, rather than just sitting there like a bump on a log!
Do you find it difficult to focus on a single task for an extended period of time?

Oh, focus... yes, well, that's another thing altogether. It's funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my friend Martha about this the other day after our church committee meeting. We're on the planning committee for the annual spring bazaar, you see, and it's a lovely event, we sell baked goods and those little crocheted potholders Martha makes—she's incredibly talented with a crochet hook, I've always admired that because I could never quite get the hang of the tension. But anyway, at the meetings, I'll sit down with my notepad, all ready to take notes and pay attention to what Pastor Davis is saying about the schedule or the budget. 

And I start out just fine! I really do. I'm listening, I'm nodding along, I'm looking right at whoever is speaking. But then... I don't know, it's like my brain just decides to go for a little stroll without telling me. After a little while, maybe ten or fifteen minutes, I'll suddenly realize that Pastor Davis is asking if everyone agrees with the new table layout, and I haven't heard a single word he said for the last five minutes. It's the same thing with reading, too. I'll sit down on Sunday morning with my cup of decaf and the church bulletin, meaning to read through the announcements and see who needs prayers this week. I'll read the first couple of paragraphs, and then my eyes are still moving over the words, but my mind is off wondering if I need to buy more flour for my pound cake, or noticing that the carpet in the hallway really needs a good vacuuming. 

Next thing I know, I've reached the bottom of the page, and I realize I’ve missed half of what was printed! I couldn't tell you a single name on the prayer list or what time the youth group is meeting if my life depended on it. I have to go back and read the whole thing over again, sometimes two or three times, just to actually absorb the information. It's terribly frustrating, really. I try so hard to just lock my brain onto one thing, especially when it's important church business or reading something I actually want to read, but it just slips away like water through a sieve. It's not that I don't care about what's being said or read, it's just that staying tuned in for a long stretch feels almost impossible sometimes.
Did you experience this restlessness and difficulty sitting still when you were a child?

Oh, as a child? Goodness, yes. If my mother were still alive—bless her heart, she passed away back in ninety-eight—but if she were here, she’d talk your ear off about it! We went to this lovely little elementary school, the kind that still had those heavy wooden desks where the chair is attached right to the table part, you know the ones? They had the little inkwell holes at the top even though we only ever used those thick yellow pencils. 

But yes, even way back then in grade school, I was exactly the same way. I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was a very proper lady who wore these beautiful pleated skirts, and she used to have to call my mother in for conferences. And she would always tell my mother that I was a bright girl, but that I was just terribly scattered. That was the word she always used, "scattered." Because I was always, always losing my papers. I'd do my spelling homework and shove it into that little cubby under the desk, and by the time she asked us to hand it in, it had just vanished into thin air! 

And the wiggling, oh my. Mrs. Gable would tell my mother that I was constantly wiggling in my seat before I had even finished my work. I just couldn't bear to sit in that hard wooden chair for the whole arithmetic lesson. I’d be shifting around, tapping my shoes on the floor, and I had a terrible habit of talking out of turn, too. I'd just blurt out the answer or start chatting with the girl next to me, Mary-Ellen, before Mrs. Gable even called on me. My mother used to say I had ants in my pants, and she’d try to get me to sit still at the dinner table at home, especially on Sundays when we had a nice roast, but I’d just eat my peas as fast as humanly possible so I could be excused to go run around in the yard. So, yes, it’s definitely not a new thing at all. It’s just how I’ve always been, ever since I was a little girl in pigtails, just a motor constantly running and losing track of my little assignments!
Have you ever had to stop or significantly cut back on any activities, such as gardening or your church committee work, because of your difficulty sitting still or focusing?

Stop altogether? Oh, goodness, no, I wouldn't say I've had to just pack it in and quit. I've never been a quitter, I like to stay involved, you know, keep my hands busy. But... well, I suppose things have definitely changed. It’s... to be perfectly honest with you, it has started causing some real strain. Yes, actual strain, which just breaks my heart a little bit to admit. 

It's mostly at home with George, and over at the community center. You see, I help out with the senior luncheons at the center—we do them on the second Tuesday of every month, usually a lovely catered affair. Sometimes we do chicken salad croissants, sometimes a nice hot baked ziti if the weather is turning chilly like it does in November. But lately, the other volunteers... well, they just can’t count on me to keep the plans straight. I hate to say it, but it’s true. I’ll be in charge of calling the caterer to confirm the headcount, and I’ll get distracted by reorganizing the linen closet or chatting with someone in the hallway, and then the caterer doesn't get the final numbers until the absolute last minute. Or I'll mix up the delivery times entirely! 

So now, it's gotten to the point where they feel like they can't trust me to handle it on my own without someone checking behind me. Susan—she's the head of the luncheon committee now, ever since Betty moved to Florida—Susan is always hovering. She means well, but she's always saying, "Did you write that down? Let me just look at your clipboard to make sure." 

And George does the exact same thing here at the house. If we have a plumber coming, or if we're supposed to go to our grandson's piano recital, George is constantly double-checking my calendar. He'll ask me three times if I actually called the repairman, because he knows I might have gotten sidetracked pulling weeds in the garden and just forgotten to make the call altogether. It's terribly frustrating, really, to feel like everyone is constantly looking over my shoulder and babysitting me. But I suppose they feel like they have to, because I just can't seem to keep all those plans straight without making a mess of things!
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Impulse? Oh, goodness no, I don't think I do that at all. Actually, it's quite the opposite when it comes to making decisions or doing things out of the blue. I mean, I know I just told you how I lose track of things and forget my lists, but that's just my brain floating away, not me just... jumping off a cliff without looking, so to speak. 

It's funny you ask, though, because my sister-in-law, Brenda—George's younger sister, she lives over in Scottsdale now, she moved there for the dry air—she is exactly like that. Just entirely impulsive! I remember back in... oh, it must have been two thousand and four, she bought a bright red convertible just because she drove past the dealership on a Tuesday afternoon and liked the color. Didn't even consult her husband! Just signed the papers right then and there. Can you imagine? I could never, ever do something like that. My heart would just pound right out of my chest. 

I'm actually quite cautious when it comes to taking action. I like to think things through, sometimes probably a bit too much, if you ask George. Like last month, we needed to replace the toaster oven because the old one just stopped heating evenly—it was burning the edges of my toast while the middle was still practically bread—and I spent three whole days reading all the different descriptions online, comparing the ones with the turn-dials to the ones with the digital buttons. George was ready to just drive down to the Walmart and buy the very first one he saw on the shelf, but I just had to make sure I wasn't making a hasty choice. I need to know exactly what I'm getting into. So, no, even though I might be a bit of a scatterbrain with my schedule and my notes, I certainly don't just act on impulse. I always try to think things through very carefully... even if I do get a little distracted while I'm doing the thinking!
Have you felt like your restlessness and difficulty focusing have significantly interfered with your relationships or daily life?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago—it really has started causing some very real strain, yes. It's exactly what I was mentioning about George and the folks over at the community center. It just... it breaks my heart, it really does. Because when you've been married to a man for forty-seven years—George and I had our anniversary back in April, we went to that nice seafood place out on Route 9, the one with the lovely nautical theme—you want to feel like an equal partner, you know? 

But instead, it's like he has to be my manager. And the exact same thing goes for the ladies at the center. It interferes with everything because they just can’t count on me to keep our plans straight without someone checking behind me. I can see the look in their eyes, Doctor. Susan will get that tight little smile she does when she's trying to be polite, but I know she's thinking, "Oh, here we go again, she's messed up the schedule." 

And George, bless him, he tries to be patient, but I can hear him sighing from the other room when he has to ask me for the third time if I actually mailed the water bill or if it's still sitting under a pile of gardening catalogs on the kitchen counter. Which, more often than not, it is! So, yes, it definitely interferes. It makes me feel like I'm just not a reliable person anymore, and I've always prided myself on being a good neighbor and a good wife. But this whole business of everyone having to constantly double-check my every move and babysit my schedule... well, it just puts a heavy cloud over my daily life and my relationships, it really does.
Have you experienced this restlessness and difficulty focusing in most areas of your life, such as at home, in social situations, and during leisure activities, for as long as you can remember?

For as long as I can remember? Oh, heavens, yes. I mean, I know sometimes people get to be my age and they start getting a little forgetful, and folks just chalk it up to getting older, but... well, this isn't that. It really isn't. It has always been this way, in absolutely everything I do, whether I'm at the house, or out with my friends, or just trying to sit and knit a sweater. 

In fact, it goes all the way back to when I was just a little girl. Even back in grade school—oh, I must have been in the third or fourth grade, I had Mrs. Gable, she was a lovely woman who always wore these beautiful floral blouses—anyway, even back then, my teachers told my mother the exact same things. They would pull her aside at the parent-teacher conferences and say, "She’s such a bright girl, she really is, but she is just so scattered!" 

And it was true! I was always losing my papers. My mother would buy me those nice folders with the little pockets on the inside, but my spelling homework would still end up crumpled at the very bottom of my bookbag, or I'd leave it on the kitchen table right next to my cereal bowl. And I was terribly chatty, always talking out of turn during the lessons. I just couldn't seem to hold a thought in—if it popped into my head, out it came! And sitting still? Oh, forget about it. I was constantly wiggling and squirming around in my little wooden seat, just itching to get up before I had even finished my arithmetic work. 

My poor mother, she tried so hard to keep me organized, but it was like trying to catch the wind in a jar. So, yes, Doctor, to answer your question... this restlessness, this... this scattered feeling where I can't just focus and stay put, it’s not a new development at all. It’s followed me around for my entire life, really. Every single bit of it.
Do you often feel like you're constantly 'on the go' or like you're driven by a motor, even when you're not necessarily trying to accomplish anything?

Oh, a motor... yes, that is exactly it. That is exactly what it feels like! George always says to me, he says, "Sweetheart, where on earth is the fire?" Because I really do feel like I’m always up and moving, just constantly on the go, even when there is absolutely no reason for it. 

Take a Sunday, for example. Sunday is supposed to be our quiet day. We come home from morning service, George settles into his brown leather recliner to watch the golf tournament on the television, and I tell myself, "Today, I am just going to sit and relax." But... well, I just can't do it. My body won't let me. I'll sit on the sofa for maybe two minutes, and then that little motor you mentioned just starts humming away inside me, and I have to get up. 

Even on a quiet day like that, I end up bouncing all over the house. I'll wander into the kitchen and start looking at the garden club list—because Susan and I are supposed to be organizing the spring planting for the beds out front of the library, and we really need to decide between the petunias and the marigolds this year. But right in the middle of trying to read the list, I'll spot my knitting bag sitting over by the armchair. So I'll leave the list on the counter and go over to the knitting bag, thinking I should really work on the cardigan I'm making for my grandniece. I'll pull out the yarn, maybe do three or four stitches, and then suddenly I'm thinking about our travel papers. 

George and I are looking into taking one of those lovely bus tours down to Branson in the fall, you see, and we have all these brochures and booking forms. So I'll put the knitting needles down on the cushion and go dig through the travel papers to see if the hotel has a continental breakfast. And before you know it, hours have gone by, I've been on my feet the entire afternoon just buzzing from room to room, and I haven't really finished any one thing! The garden list is still sitting there, the sweater is missing a sleeve, and I still don't know about the breakfast in Branson. 

I'm not even trying to accomplish anything big, I'm really not! It’s not like I'm doing a deep spring cleaning or anything like that. It’s just this... this restless energy. I just can't seem to turn it off and sit still. My feet just always want to be moving onto the next thing, and then the next, and then the next...
Have you ever felt like your restlessness and difficulty focusing have significantly impacted your ability to maintain relationships or hold a job?

Well, Doctor, I know we touched on this just a little bit ago, but yes, absolutely. It's exactly like I was saying about my George and the community center. Now, as for a job, I haven't worked an official paying job in years and years—I’ve mostly just focused on keeping the house and doing my volunteer work since I retired—but in terms of my relationships? Oh, it has started causing some very real strain at home, and at the center, too. 

It’s just so frustrating for everyone, because my husband and the other volunteers... well, they simply can’t count on me to keep our plans straight without someone checking behind me. Like with Susan and the garden club, or when we do the charity bake sales, someone always feels like they have to call me the night before to say, "Now remember, we're meeting at ten, not eleven, and don't forget the change box." And George is always having to peek over my shoulder to make sure I actually wrote our appointments down on the big floral calendar in the kitchen, rather than just jotting them on a scrap of paper that I'll inevitably lose at the bottom of my purse. 

It really does put a heavy strain on things, having people constantly double-checking my every move because they know I can't keep the schedule straight on my own. You want your husband to be your partner, not your supervisor, you know? And you want your friends to trust you with responsibilities! But when they always have to follow up and check behind me... well, it just makes things very tense.
Do you often find yourself doing things without thinking them through?

Doing things without thinking them through? Oh... no, I don't think so. No, I wouldn't say I do that. If anything, I think about things a little too much! George always jokes that if I have a decision to make, we’d better pack a lunch. 

I really don't just jump into things or act rashly. Just the other day, for instance, I was down at the department store—they were having their big spring white sale, you know, where all the bed linens and bath items are marked down. Well, I needed some new hand towels for the guest bathroom, because the old ones are getting a bit frayed at the edges, and my sister Martha is coming to visit from Ohio next month. So I stood there in the aisle, and I must have looked at the seafoam green towels and the pale yellow towels for a good twenty minutes. 

I picked them up, I felt the cotton loops to see how thick they were, I looked at the washing instructions... and then I stood there thinking about the wallpaper in the guest bathroom. It has these little yellow daisies on it, so I thought, well, the yellow would match perfectly, but the green might provide a nice, crisp contrast. I turned it over and over in my head. I didn't just grab a towel and throw it in my cart without a second thought! I thought about it from every single angle. 

And it's like that with just about everything I do. I don't just blurt things out or make sudden choices out of nowhere. I mean, yes, like we talked about, I might get completely sidetracked while I'm in the middle of making the decision—I think I actually ended up wandering over to the perfume counter to smell the new Estée Lauder before I even put a towel in my basket—but the acting without thinking part? No, I definitely wouldn't say that fits me. My mind is always full of thoughts about whatever I'm doing, probably too many thoughts all at once!
Have you ever had a period in your life where you felt completely free of this restless feeling and able to focus without any difficulty?

A period where I felt completely free of it? Oh my... well, let me just think back. No. No, I really don't believe I ever have. It feels like this is just how I've always been, ever since I was a little girl. 

I mean, I think about my childhood, growing up back in the early sixties, and things were so different then, you know? The classrooms were so strict, and you were expected to just sit with your hands folded on your desk for hours on end. Well, I just couldn't do it. Even back in grade school, oh, it was the exact same story as it is today. I remember my third-grade teacher—Mrs. Gable, she was a lovely woman, always wore these beautiful pearl brooches—she would sit down with my mother at parent-teacher conferences and she'd say, "Now, your daughter is a very bright girl, she really is, but she is just so terribly scattered." 

And she was right! My mother used to get so exasperated with me, bless her heart. I was always, always losing my spelling papers or my homework assignments. I'd put them in my bookbag and they'd just vanish into thin air, or I'd leave them on the kitchen table. And the wiggling! Oh my goodness, I simply could not sit still. I'd be wiggling and squirming in my little wooden seat, just itching to get up and do something else before I had even finished my arithmetic worksheet. And I was always getting shushed for talking out of turn, because a thought would pop into my head about a bird outside the window or what we were having for lunch, and out it would come before I even remembered I was supposed to raise my hand. 

So, no, Doctor... I don't think there was ever a magical time where I was free of this restless feeling or could just sit down and focus perfectly. It's just always been my normal, from Mrs. Gable's classroom right up to my living room with George today. I've always just been a busy bee, buzzing around, losing my papers, and trying to keep up with myself.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or blurting out answers before they finish speaking?

Oh, well... yes. Yes, I suppose I do. George—my husband, you know—he brings this up quite a lot, actually. He’s always saying, "Now let me finish, Martha," or well, my name isn't Martha, that's my sister, but you know what I mean! He says I cut him off right in the middle of his sentences. And it’s not that I mean to be rude, really it isn’t! It’s just that... well, we’ll be sitting at the breakfast table, and he’ll start telling me about something he read in the morning paper, maybe an article about the city council or the new zoning laws—he follows all of that so closely, you see. 

And as he's talking, a thought will just pop into my head. Maybe it's about the zoning laws, or maybe it reminds me of something I need to ask him about the gutters, because they really do need cleaning before the spring rains start. And the thing is, Doctor, if I don't say it right that very second, the thought is just gone! Poof! Like a dandelion in the wind. I get so terribly anxious that I'll forget what I was going to say, so out it comes, right over whatever he was trying to tell me. 

And it’s not just with George, either. I do the exact same thing when we have our group planning meetings down at the community center. Oh, it can be quite embarrassing, to be honest. Susan will be right in the middle of explaining her idea for the spring raffle baskets—she always has such lovely ideas, last year she did a whole basket just with local honeys and jams—and I’ll just blurt out something about the ticket prices before she’s even finished her thought. I can see the look on her face, that little tight-lipped smile she gets. But again, it’s just this overwhelming feeling that if I wait my turn, the idea will completely vanish from my mind by the time she’s done speaking. So I just jump right in, and then of course I feel awful about it afterward. But yes, I do find myself doing that quite a bit.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for ADHD?

Diagnosed? Oh my heavens, no. No, nothing like that. You have to understand, Doctor, when I was growing up, and even when I was a young mother raising my own children back in the seventies, nobody ever really talked about things like this. If you were a bit scattered, or if you couldn't keep your house perfectly tidy—and oh, my house was always a bit of a jumble, I’d have a pile of laundry sitting on the sofa and a half-finished sewing project taking up the entire dining room table—well, people just said you were flighty. Or a daydreamer. They certainly didn't have medical names for it, and they definitely didn't give you any sort of treatment! 

I mean, I’ve been going to my regular physician, Dr. Henderson, for over forty years. He just retired last spring, actually, which was such a shame because he was a wonderful man, he delivered both of my boys. But in all those years, he never once mentioned anything about a diagnosis for... well, for the way my brain works. He’d check my blood pressure, and he’d always remind me to watch my cholesterol, especially since George’s cholesterol has been creeping up and we really try to eat heart-healthy these days—lots of oatmeal and we completely cut out the butter, which was a tough adjustment for George—but Dr. Henderson never suggested there was an actual condition I needed treatment for. 

So, no, nobody has ever diagnosed me with anything or offered me any kind of treatment. I’ve honestly just thought it was me being my usual, disorganized self all these decades!
Have you ever considered that you might have ADHD or been evaluated for it by a healthcare professional?

Considered it? Oh, my goodness, no. No, never in a million years. You see, when I hear those letters you just said, I always just picture little boys bouncing off the walls. Like my nephew’s boy, little Kevin. Oh, Kevin was a handful when he was in grade school, let me tell you. He was always climbing the curtains and running out into the street, and they did all sorts of tests on him. But the idea that a woman of my age, a seventy-year-old grandmother who just likes to knit and garden—even if my garden is a bit of a weed patch right now because I keep forgetting to pull the dandelions—could have something like that? It simply never crossed my mind. Not once. 

I always just assumed this was a character flaw, you know? A lack of discipline, or just me being a bit scatterbrained. My mother certainly thought so, and George, well, he just calls it my "quirks." He'll say, "There goes my busy bee again," when I leave the milk out on the counter. 

And as for being evaluated by a professional, well, like I was just saying about Dr. Henderson, he never did any such thing. I wouldn't even know what an evaluation for that entails! Is it a test with a pencil and paper? Or do they hook you up to some sort of machine to look at your head? Because nobody has ever done anything like that for me. I've had my heart checked, and my bone density—oh, they are very thorough about the bone density now that I'm older, they have you lay on this big table and it takes a picture, and I have to take a calcium pill every morning now, well, when I actually remember to take it, anyway—but no, no one has ever evaluated my brain or my focus. This sitting here with you is the very first time anyone has ever really asked me these kinds of questions about my life!
Do you experience these restless feelings and difficulty focusing at work, at home, and in social situations?

Well, as for work, I haven't actually held a job in years—I used to work in the cafeteria over at the middle school, but I retired back in two thousand and five. So I don't have to worry about that anymore, thank goodness! But at home and in my social groups? Oh, yes. Yes, it really is everywhere, and to be perfectly honest with you, Doctor, it has started causing some real strain lately. 

Take things at home, for instance. George—bless his heart, he really does try to be patient with me—but he gets so flustered because he just can't count on me to keep our plans straight anymore. Just last week, we were supposed to go to his brother’s house for a Sunday roast, and I completely double-booked us with the neighborhood watch meeting because I couldn't focus long enough to check the planner. Now he feels like he has to constantly check the calendar on the fridge—you know, the one with the little magnetic dry-erase marker that always seems to go missing—and he’s always checking behind me. He'll look over my shoulder and say, "Are you absolutely sure you wrote that time down right, dear?" It makes me feel like a child, but I can't really blame him. 

And it’s the exact same story down at the community center. It used to just be a bit of a running joke that I was the scatterbrained one of the bunch, but lately, it’s causing genuine tension with the ladies. The other volunteers, like Susan and Mary, they’re trying to plan the spring bake sale right now. I was supposed to coordinate the volunteer shifts, but I got so restless trying to sit down and focus on the sign-up sheet that I kept getting up to water the lobby plants, and then I started reorganizing the folding chairs in the closet... and the schedule ended up a complete jumble. Two people showed up to run the cash box at the same time, and nobody was there to cut the pies! 

Now, I can just tell they don't trust me to handle the important tasks. Susan actually went back through my whole list and called everyone to double-check their times. It feels awful, it really does. It's just getting to the point where my husband and the other volunteers feel like they can't rely on me without someone coming along right behind me to make sure I actually finished what I started.
Do you often find yourself acting on impulse without fully considering the consequences?

Acting on impulse? Well, I suppose... I mean, I don't think I do things that are terribly dangerous or anything like that. I'm not out there skydiving or buying sports cars on a whim, heavens no. George would have a fit if I did anything like that! He’s always been the sensible one, always thinking three steps ahead, while I just sort of... well, I just sort of go with the flow, I guess you could say. 

But as for doing things without thinking them through first... I really don't think so. I mean, sometimes I might buy a new type of yarn at the craft store just because the color caught my eye—oh, they had this absolutely gorgeous variegated blue the other day, it reminded me of the ocean in Maine where we went for our honeymoon, but then I got it home and realized I didn't have a pattern for it, and it was a bit too bulky for the needles I prefer to use. So now it's just sitting in my knitting basket. But I wouldn't call that acting on impulse in a bad way, would you? Just a little treat. 

And, well, I do sometimes speak my mind a bit quickly. Like at the garden club last month, when Martha was going on and on about her prize-winning hydrangeas, and I might have blurted out that they looked a bit droopy this year before I really thought about how it would sound. She was quite offended, and I felt terrible afterward, I really did. I had to bake her a batch of my lemon squares to apologize. But I don't think that's what you mean, is it? You mean doing things that have real, serious consequences, right? Because I really don't think I do that. I try to be careful, I really do, even if my mind is always going in a hundred different directions at once.

patient.answer:
Oh, that is a very good question. You know, I suppose people might look at me and think I’m just trying to be a busy bee and get a million chores done, but... well, honestly, it’s really because I just can't seem to settle. 

It's the strangest thing. If I have to sit still for too long—like if my husband puts on one of his long history documentaries in the evening, he just loves those World War II ones on PBS, and I do try to sit and watch them with him because it’s nice to spend that time together—but after maybe twenty or thirty minutes, I get this... this stirred-up feeling inside. It's almost like a little motor humming, and I just feel like I absolutely need to stand up and straighten something or go check on something. 

I'll tell him I'm just going to the kitchen for a glass of water, but really I just need to get up and go fluff the throw pillows in the den, or check if I remembered to lock the back door, or see if the African violets on the windowsill need watering. And once I'm up, of course, that's when I start bouncing around again. So it's not really that I have some grand master plan to be incredibly productive, though Lord knows there is always something to clean or organize in that house. It's more that my body just decides it's had enough of the chair and I have to move. Even at church, if the pastor's sermon goes on a bit too long, I get that exact same stirred-up feeling in my chest and I catch myself shifting around, just waiting until we can finally stand up for the last hymn. I just can't seem to turn that feeling off, no matter how much I tell myself to just relax.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are associated with any emotional distress

Oh, anxious? Worried? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like a... like a dread or a fear that something terrible is going to happen, you know? It's not like when I couldn't find my granddaughter at the county fair that one time—now that was anxiety! My heart was pounding out of my chest, I was sweating, I couldn't breathe right until I saw her over by the cotton candy stand with her uncle. No, this feeling when I'm sitting still, it's completely different from that. 

It's really just... physical, I suppose? Like an itch you can't scratch, or like when you've had way too much coffee, though I only ever have my one cup of decaf in the mornings now because regular coffee gives me terrible heartburn. But it's just this restless energy. I don't sit there thinking, "Oh dear, did I leave the stove on?" or "What if the roof leaks?" I just sit there and my legs want to move, and my arms want to do something, and my brain just says, "Up, up, up, time to go!" 

So it's not a worry. It's not my mind spinning with bad thoughts. It's just my body absolutely refusing to be still. My husband, bless him, he'll ask me sometimes, "What's wrong, dear? What are you fretting about?" when he sees me fidgeting during his programs. And I always have to tell him, "I'm not fretting about a single thing, George! I just can't sit in this recliner for one more second!" So, no, definitely not anxious, just... terribly, terribly restless.

patient.answer:
Irritable? Oh, goodness, no, I wouldn't say irritable. I mean, I don't get snappy or mean with anyone just because I have to sit still. George, my husband, he’s the one who gets irritable if his back is acting up and he can’t get out to his woodworking shop in the garage, but me? No, I don't get cross. 

It’s just... well, like I was saying, it’s just that restless, humming feeling. I might sigh a bit, or shift my weight, or start tapping my foot—which I know can probably be a bit annoying to anyone sitting next to me, especially in a quiet church pew or when George is trying to listen to the narrator on his shows. But it's not because I'm mad or frustrated. I don't sit there feeling angry that I can't get up. I just sit there feeling like I *have* to get up. 

There was this one time, oh, it must have been last Thanksgiving, when my daughter insisted I sit at the head of the table and just let everyone else serve the meal and clear the plates. She meant well, she really did, she kept saying, "Mom, you cooked the turkey, you just sit and enjoy." And I tried, I really did try to just sit there while they bustled around clearing the good china—which, by the way, I only bring out for Thanksgiving and Easter because it has to be hand-washed, and nobody wants to do that every day. But anyway, as I sat there watching them, I wasn't irritable with them for making me sit. I just felt that motor running inside me, telling me to get up and help scrape the plates or put the leftover stuffing in the Tupperware. 

So, no, I wouldn't use the word irritable at all. I don't lose my temper or feel grumpy about it. It's really just that my body is so very eager to be doing *something*, anything at all, rather than just sitting there like a bump on a log!

patient.answer:
Oh, focus... yes, well, that's another thing altogether. It's funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my friend Martha about this the other day after our church committee meeting. We're on the planning committee for the annual spring bazaar, you see, and it's a lovely event, we sell baked goods and those little crocheted potholders Martha makes—she's incredibly talented with a crochet hook, I've always admired that because I could never quite get the hang of the tension. But anyway, at the meetings, I'll sit down with my notepad, all ready to take notes and pay attention to what Pastor Davis is saying about the schedule or the budget. 

And I start out just fine! I really do. I'm listening, I'm nodding along, I'm looking right at whoever is speaking. But then... I don't know, it's like my brain just decides to go for a little stroll without telling me. After a little while, maybe ten or fifteen minutes, I'll suddenly realize that Pastor Davis is asking if everyone agrees with the new table layout, and I haven't heard a single word he said for the last five minutes. It's the same thing with reading, too. I'll sit down on Sunday morning with my cup of decaf and the church bulletin, meaning to read through the announcements and see who needs prayers this week. I'll read the first couple of paragraphs, and then my eyes are still moving over the words, but my mind is off wondering if I need to buy more flour for my pound cake, or noticing that the carpet in the hallway really needs a good vacuuming. 

Next thing I know, I've reached the bottom of the page, and I realize I’ve missed half of what was printed! I couldn't tell you a single name on the prayer list or what time the youth group is meeting if my life depended on it. I have to go back and read the whole thing over again, sometimes two or three times, just to actually absorb the information. It's terribly frustrating, really. I try so hard to just lock my brain onto one thing, especially when it's important church business or reading something I actually want to read, but it just slips away like water through a sieve. Oh, as a child? Goodness, yes. If my mother were still alive—bless her heart, she passed away back in ninety-eight—but if she were here, she’d talk your ear off about it! We went to this lovely little elementary school, the kind that still had those heavy wooden desks where the chair is attached right to the table part, you know the ones? They had the little inkwell holes at the top even though we only ever used those thick yellow pencils. 

But yes, even way back then in grade school, I was exactly the same way. I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was a very proper lady who wore these beautiful pleated skirts, and she used to have to call my mother in for conferences. And she would always tell my mother that I was a bright girl, but that I was just terribly scattered. That was the word she always used, "scattered." Because I was always, always losing my papers. I'd do my spelling homework and shove it into that little cubby under the desk, and by the time she asked us to hand it in, it had just vanished into thin air! 

And the wiggling, oh my. Mrs. Gable would tell my mother that I was constantly wiggling in my seat before I had even finished my work. I just couldn't bear to sit in that hard wooden chair for the whole arithmetic lesson. I’d be shifting around, tapping my shoes on the floor, and I had a terrible habit of talking out of turn, too. Impulse? Oh, goodness no, I don't think I do that at all. Actually, it's quite the opposite when it comes to making decisions or doing things out of the blue. I mean, I know I just told you how I lose track of things and forget my lists, but that's just my brain floating away, not me just... jumping off a cliff without looking, so to speak. 

It's funny you ask, though, because my sister-in-law, Brenda—George's younger sister, she lives over in Scottsdale now, she moved there for the dry air—she is exactly like that. Just entirely impulsive! I remember back in... oh, it must have been two thousand and four, she bought a bright red convertible just because she drove past the dealership on a Tuesday afternoon and liked the color. Didn't even consult her husband! Just signed the papers right then and there. Can you imagine? I could never, ever do something like that. My heart would just pound right out of my chest. 

I'm actually quite cautious when it comes to taking action. I like to think things through, sometimes probably a bit too much, if you ask George. Like last month, we needed to replace the toaster oven because the old one just stopped heating evenly—it was burning the edges of my toast while the middle was still practically bread—and I spent three whole days reading all the different descriptions online, comparing the ones with the turn-dials to the ones with the digital buttons.
